title: Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’
description: Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan’s largest telecom operator, announced 10 new investments at its “Chunghwa Telecom Content Slate and Partnership Showcase,”
body:
Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan’s largest telecom operator, announced 10 new investments at its “Chunghwa Telecom Content Slate and Partnership Showcase,” spanning film, TV and music projects as well as stakes in two production companies. 

	The company pitched the slate as a way to back Taiwanese original IP and link local creators with partners abroad. The event was held at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF), which Chunghwa has sponsored for five consecutive years. Taiwan’s Minister of Culture Li Yuan attended, alongside Chunghwa chief business officer and senior executive VP Lin Wen-chiyh, consumer business group president Hu Hsueh-hai and representatives from the presenting teams.
	

	“Chunghwa Telecom is like a pyramid,” Li said. “I am grateful that, beyond building a strong foundation through its thriving core business, the company is also willing to invest at the very top of the pyramid, supporting film and television professionals as they continue moving forward and creating even better work.”

	The slate includes four scripted series: police crime drama “Gunshot,” made with PTS Taigi TV, the Taiwanese-language channel of public broadcaster PTS, and S11 Partners; family fantasy “Yesterday’s Daughter, Tomorrow’s Mother,” from producer Phoebe Ma and director Hung Tzu-peng; fantasy adventure “Guides to the World Below,” adapted from a popular Taiwanese comic; and “C’est la Vie,” an urban drama about food and women’s personal growth, with actress Esther Liu as executive producer. Chunghwa has also invested in “Next Z Chef,” billed as Taiwan’s first cooking competition show for young people.
	

	Film investments include “Demon of the East: Black Condo,” a horror project tied to a cinematic universe that crosses four Asian countries, and “Call of Lobster,” which won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF’s 2024 pitching sessions and has since been selected for the Culture Ministry’s first international flagship cohort under its Great Voyage Project.

	The investments also extend to music, including “Speak in Silence,” an Asian tour by Taiwanese indie band Shallow Levée. The tour will run to about 50 shows in Taiwan and eight other countries across Asia.

	Alongside project financing, Chunghwa and Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative have taken equity positions in DaMou Entertainment and Horiza Creations. DaMou has produced series including “The World Between Us II” and “Wave Makers.” Horiza uses community engagement and crowdfunding to gauge what audiences want.

	“Chunghwa Telecom is more than just a platform operator; we are also a driving force behind the long-term development of the content industry,” Lin said. “Moving forward, we will continue to connect funding, creative talent, and domestic and international partners, leveraging our group’s resources and industry partnerships to help Taiwanese content reach international markets.”

	Chunghwa-backed films “Arrested Memory” and “The Photo From 1977” received a combined 12 nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards. The company operates mobile and broadband networks as well as the MOD IPTV service and the Hami Video streaming platform, which together have more than 3 million subscribers.

schema.headline: Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’

title: James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve
description: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars wh
body:
As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007. 

	Both British actors certainly have the acting pedigree to play the suave spy, taking up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. They also have a keen awareness of what it takes to work in major franchise fare: Pattinson stars as Batman for DC Studios and is an alum of both the “Twilight” and “Harry Potter” franchises; meanwhile, Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman movies and starred in the 2010s “X-Men” prequel trilogy. He next stars in the Amazon MGM Studios movie “How to Rob a Bank,” in theaters next Friday, Nov. 13. Pattinson also has the Denis Villeneuve factor on his side, after starring in the filmmaker’s upcoming epic “Dune: Part Three.” 
	

	Last year, Amazon MGM Studios tapped Villeneuve as the franchise’s next director, with “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight hired to write the script. Getting Bond 26 off the ground has been a top priority for the property’s new stewards, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

	Since then, nearly every 30-something British actor’s name has been bandied about in the U.K. and U.S. press, with rumored top contenders including Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Variety has learned that Harry Styles has had discussions about the part, and Theo James also hasn’t been ruled out.

	Pierce Brosnan, the Bond of the 90s, recently gave his stamp of approval to Turner, while Gary Oldman threw his weight behind Lowden, his “Slow Horses” co-star. (Oldman also claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made.)
	

	Amazon declined to comment on the casting rumors.

schema.headline: James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve

title: Bill Maher Rubs Salt in Trump’s Midterms Wound: ‘Donnie, Are You OK?’
description: While his HBO counterpart John Oliver issued an urgent warning about voting GOP during the midterms, Bill Maher spent the majority of his time in t
body:
While his HBO counterpart John Oliver issued an urgent warning about voting GOP during the midterms, Bill Maher spent the majority of his time in the lead-up to the critical election dining with the Trump at the White House (and then bickering with him publicly), conducting an embarrassingly softball interview with Trump’s former press secretary Karoline Leavitt and platforming Kid Rock’s racist rants against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
	

	And so, following a blue tsunami that saw the Democrats wrest back control of Congress in startlingly dominant fashion, the increasingly illiberal pundit dedicated Friday night’s episode of “Real Time” to “gloat” about the Dems’ big night — and make some gay jokes.


	“Republicans lost bigly. There’s no other way to put it. And, great! Now I’m never going to get that check for $5,000,” joked Maher, adding, “In 2016, Lindsey Graham said, ‘If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed… and we will deserve it,’ and it just shows gays are always ten years ahead of everybody.” (Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina, passed away in July.)

	He wasn’t done. “Well, look, I hate to gloat, but sorry, I have to do a little bit because everybody was hedging about this election,” Maher said, before pointing to a series clips of himself on “Real Time” and various cable news programs predicting that the Democrats would deliver a “historical thumping” to the Republicans during the midterms.

	“Here’s something I could not have predicted: Trump’s reaction to the election. He said, ‘Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job,’” offered Maher, before looking directly into the camera and addressing his sparring partner: “Donnie, are you OK? I know we’ve been feuding. You sound unwell. You’re not even going to fake it was rigged?”

schema.headline: Bill Maher Rubs Salt in Trump’s Midterms Wound: ‘Donnie, Are You OK?’

title: ‘The Remarried Empress’ Becomes Most-Viewed Local Original Premiere Ever on Disney+ and Hulu
description: Korean fantasy romance “The Remarried Empress” has set a new high for Disney+ and Hulu. Based on views across the three days after its Nov. 3 launc
body:
Korean fantasy romance “The Remarried Empress” has set a new high for Disney+ and Hulu. Based on views across the three days after its Nov. 3 launch, it is the biggest premiere ever for a local original on the platforms worldwide.

	The series is also the No. 1 Korean title premiere in more than 50 markets. These include the U.S., the U.K., Canada, Mexico, Chile, France, Spain, Germany, Australia and New Zealand.


	The show had been slated to bow on Nov. 4. Disney+ instead released it a day ahead of schedule as a gesture of gratitude to its fanbase.
	

	The show is adapted from the Naver Webtoon series of the same name. It centers on Empress Navier and Emperor Sovieshu, rulers of the Eastern Empire, whose marriage starts to crack as tensions mount across their realm. Things unravel when Sovieshu falls for Rashta, an escaped slave, and goes to extreme lengths to win her over.

	Navier refuses to give up her dignity. She agrees to what the emperor wants, as long as she is free to wed Heinrey, crown prince of the rival Western Kingdom. The fallout puts the entire empire at risk as Navier fights to take back her power.

	Shin Mina (“Karma,” “Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha”) plays Navier, with Ju Jihoon (“Light Shop,” “The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call”) as Sovieshu, Lee Jongsuk (“Big Mouth”) as Heinrey and Lee Seyoung (“The Red Sleeve,” “The Crowned Clown”) as Rashta. Cho Suwon (“Still 17,” “Pinocchio”) directs from a screen adaptation by Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol.

	Anticipation for the series had been running high. Preview screenings at the Busan International Film Festival sold out, and the payoff trailer racked up 13 million views across YouTube and social platforms within 48 hours. The source webtoon has drawn close to 3 billion views since it first came out.
	

	The first four episodes are streaming now. Two more will arrive each Wednesday starting Nov. 11, leading up to the finale on Nov. 25, exclusively on Disney+ and Hulu.

	Outside the U.S., Hulu operates as an entertainment banner within Disney+. In the U.S., subscribers on bundle plans can access Hulu programming without leaving the Disney+ app.

schema.headline: ‘The Remarried Empress’ Becomes Most-Viewed Local Original Premiere Ever on Disney+ and Hulu

title: Chang Chen Urges Emerging Taiwanese Actors to ‘Be Like Water’ at Taiwan Creative Content Fest Golden Horse Showcase
description: Chang Chen, chair of the Taipei Golden Horse Film Festival Executive Committee and last year’s Golden Horse best leading actor winner for “Lucky Lu
body:
Chang Chen, chair of the Taipei Golden Horse Film Festival Executive Committee and last year’s Golden Horse best leading actor winner for “Lucky Lu,” advised six of Taiwan’s rising performers on working across different film sets at a Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) showcase in Taipei.

	The “TCCF x The Golden Horse Awards: Taiwan Emerging Actors Showcase” featured Bai Xiao-ying, Ho Man-xi, Rosen, Jimmy Liu, Ma Shih-yuan and Lin Yi-ting. All are nominees or winners of Best New Performer at the Golden Horse Awards, Taiwan’s top honors for Chinese-language cinema. The event aimed to connect performers with international creative teams, investors and media.
	

	The lineup drew from two consecutive Golden Horse Awards cycles. Bai and Ho are nominees for this year’s Best New Performer award for “Girl” and “Sunshine Women’s Choir,” respectively. Ma won the award last year for “Left-Handed Girl,” while Rosen, Liu and Lin were nominated for “Marching Boys,” “Blind Love” and “A Dance With Rainbows,” respectively.

	Bai, who began acting at 6, is now a university student studying film. She greeted the audience in Mandarin and Japanese and said she had trained in traditional Chinese martial arts for a decade. Ho, who described herself as slow to warm up, serious and full of contrasts, drew on her extensive dance training; she hopes to take on a suspense action film or other physically forceful roles.

	Liu said he had practiced taekwondo for seven years. “At this stage, I feel it’s more important to light up others than to light up myself,” Lin said.
	

	Ma said acting helps her find an outlet for pressure. “When you give yourself completely to a role, audiences can feel your sincerity,” she said. “It can give others strength and help you understand yourself better.”

	Rosen spoke about his love of nature and how acting gives him the chance to pick up new skills for each role. While preparing for one project, he learned Western fencing and later entered a competition, where he won a bout.

	Asked what roles they hoped to try next, Bai, Ma and Liu said they wanted to break away from familiar casting and try comedy or villains.

	Chang praised the six performers. “Actors have to be like water, changing shape to fit the vessel,” he said. Asked about international productions, he said each set has its own atmosphere, whether led by Wong Kar-wai or Hou Hsiao-hsien. Actors, he added, need to understand how much room each director and production team gives them.

	“Ang Lee once told me that actors should read autobiographies of people with different personalities. Our job is to inhabit the lives of many different characters through our performances,” Chang said. “Taipei may not have Hollywood’s industry ecosystem, but we’re working in a place we know, and that can help us do our best work.”

schema.headline: Chang Chen Urges Emerging Taiwanese Actors to ‘Be Like Water’ at Taiwan Creative Content Fest Golden Horse Showcase

title: ‘Fire Country’ and ‘Sheriff Country’ Bosses Break Down the Crossover Episode, ‘Con Air’ Influences and the Potential Romance That Wasn’t on the Page
description:
Nov 6, 2026 7:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Fire Country’ and ‘Sheriff Country’ Bosses Break Down the Crossover Episode, ‘Con Air’ Influences and
body:
Nov 6, 2026 7:00pm PT	
	

	
		‘Fire Country’ and ‘Sheriff Country’ Bosses Break Down the Crossover Episode, ‘Con Air’ Influences and the Potential Romance That Wasn’t on the Page
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Darren Goldstein/CBS
	

		
	
				


	SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for “Sheriff Country” Season 2, Episode 5, “No Way In” and “Fire Country” Season 5, Episode 5, “No Way Out.” Both series stream on Paramount+.

	It was all hands on deck for the most recent crossover between CBS procedurals “Sheriff Country” and “Fire Country.” A raging wildfire sent Manny (Kevin Alejandro) and the rest of Station 42 to the Edgewater Police Department to ask Mickey (Morena Baccarin) and her squad for help evacuating residents if the flames moved closer to town. The request was made a bit awkward by the reveal that Manny and Mickey once went on a date from hell after being paired up at the police department’s annual date auction.

	There wasn’t too much time to dwell on that, as the mission was complicated by the news of a prison break. Three women inmates escaped a transport van in the midst of the fire chaos, and Mickey needed her troops to find the missing convicts instead of helping with the fire. Mickey ultimately sacrificed herself to the convicts after they were found at The Meat Up, and would only let the hostages inside go if Mickey let them take her daughter, Skye (Amanda Arcuri), with them as collateral to make it across the county border.



	

					Matt Lauria and Morena Baccarin 
									Courtesy of Darren Goldstein/CBS
	



	Skye was saved by her mom, and Manny didn’t let a bad date stop him from volunteering to drive the fire truck the trio wanted to escape in so he could help them fight the incoming flames at the top of the crossover’s second hour. The situation went from stressful to terrifying when a downed semi-truck forced Mickey to improvise and call in his crew so they could allegedly clear the truck, but also buy him and Mickey time to escape their captors. The trio realized what was going on before Mickey and Manny could fully escape, leading to a shootout and one inmate with a serious grudge trying to ax Mickey to death.


	Eventually, Boone (Matt Lauria), Bode (Max Thieriot), and the crew were able to subdue Manny and Mickey’s captors, allowing everyone to go home to their families in one piece. Manny and Mickey ended the day with a beer, and they cleared the air about their awful date. The chemistry was crackling as they shared a drink, and they weren’t the only pair with sparks flying in the two-hour crossover.

	Variety spoke to “Sheriff Country” showrunner Matt Lopez and “Fire Country” showrunner Eric Guggenheim about how they crafted this year’s action-packed crossover episodes with shows that film on opposite coasts — and what burgeoning relationships are going to extend into the rest of the season.


	
		What is the biggest logistical challenge of planning a crossover for two shows that shoot on opposite sides of Canada, with “Fire Country” filming in Vancouver, and “Sheriff Country” in Toronto?	

	Eric Guggenheim: You said it. The shows film on opposite sides of the country, and across three time zones. Scheduling is probably the biggest challenge, but it’s a fun puzzle for us to figure out. It’s a real credit to the line producers on both “Sheriff” and “Fire” that they were able to make it work. The next thing is continuity, because we shot scenes for Part 2 in Toronto before we started shooting “Fire Country” Season 5. Then we shot scenes from Part 1 in Vancouver further down the road.

	Matt Lopez: It’s definitely the scheduling. If an actor is needed in the other city for two days, you have to tack on a couple of days of travel on either end of that. That is very tricky. I know for the cast, they enjoy it, but it is hard for them with the jet lag and everything. I think they love visiting the sister show and visiting with the other cast. We do these one-offs all the time where Wes [W. Earl Brown]] will go to “Fire,” or Jake [Jordan Halloway] will go to “Sheriff,” but it feels a bit like “Avengers” when the whole gang gets together.



	

					Matt Lauria and Max Thieriot 
									Courtesy of Sergei Bachlakov/CBS
	




	
		Can you talk about the learning curve when “Fire Country” cast members have to learn how to do a sting or arrest someone properly and “Sheriff Country” actors have to deal with flames?	

	Matt Lopez: I love going over to “Fire.” Dawn, who is one of our “Sheriff” consultants, [is] a retired SWAT commander, and she’s incredible. She’s on my “Sheriff” set all the time. I love sitting with tech consultants on “Fire” and learning about everything. I think the cast loves that too. It’s just like, “Oh, that’s how the other club does it.”


	
		What made a prison break the right premise to bring the casts together for this crossover?	

	Guggenhiem: “Con Air” was certainly an inspiration. It’s funny, because there’s almost a whole subgenre of ‘90s action films that seemed to take place during weather events, whether it was rainfall, tornadoes or fires. That was also a big inspiration for us. Then throw in “Thelma & Louise,” which is another great ‘90s thriller. That’s how this idea was born, and then it was figuring out what the shape of it was. One of the things I love about this particular crossover is that there are stakes right away, but as the two-hour story progresses, the scope just keeps getting bigger and bigger. It feels like every few minutes there is a new card turned, a new obstacle, a new reveal.



	

					Morena Baccarin
									Courtesy of Darren Goldstein/CBS
	




	
		Mickey and Manny end up being the odd couple at the center of both hours. What made them the ideal pairing to put together? We haven’t seen them interact much before this.	

	Lopez: Kevin Alejandro came over and directed two episodes of Season 1 of “Sheriff Country.” I was able to see, off camera, how Morena and Kevin would josh each other and bust each other’s chops in a really fun, good-natured way. When we first sat down we looked at last year’s crossover pairings, we had unexpected pairings, like we threw Wes and Eve together. We looked at those two rosters, and asked who we wanted to see that we haven’t seen and whether there are any that we wanted to repeat. Bode and Boone have their buddy cop — speaking of ‘80s and ‘90s action movies — thing. We felt like we wanted to see that again. When it came to different pairings, Mickey and Manny came to mind.

	Joan Rater, one of the creators of both shows, told me once that there was an early outline for the “Sheriff Country” pilot where it was strongly suggested that Mickey and Manny had dated. It ended up completely falling away, but I guess it stayed in my subconscious. That turned into, “What if they went on this historically bad date?” It wasn’t like Joan’s version where they had dated for months. We morphed it into them just having the date from hell.


	
		They go from strangers who had been on one bad date to being friends — or potentially more. Should fans be reading into that final scene between them? The chemistry was palpable.	

	Guggenheim: It’s funny that you say that, because we felt the same thing watching the cut. The chemistry is off the charts, but Manny is in a committed relationship.

	Lopez: If you read the last scene on the page, it was just a friendly wrap-up. It’s two colleagues having a beer. When we saw it, it was like, “OK, there’s definitely chemistry there.” It’s interesting and fun to think about.



	

					Amanda Acuri 
									Courtesy of Darren Goldstein/CBS
	




	
		Two people who were a lot more overt with their romantic intentions were Tex (Elias Cacavas) and Skye. Can you tease what you’re setting up there and how Mickey is going to feel about it? Her daughter is going to stay sober, but she wants to date an inmate at Three Rock.	

	Lopez: We agree, they have great chemistry. The folks at the studio and the network wanted more of them. They are really, really good. It’s a pairing that we are going to see again on both shows. We were talking about this yesterday in the writers’ room. Both Mickey and Wes are going to find out about Skye’s new boyfriend. For a guy who has served two stints in a federal penitentiary, Wes is not cool with it and does not think it is a good idea for Skye to be dating an ex-con.


	
		Mickey faces an inmate in this episode who wants to kill her, but Mickey promises that she’ll try to reunite Crystal (Britney Young) with her son. Does that go out the window when Crystal still tries to kill her? They share a look before Crystal is taken away that says maybe Mickey still has it in her to try.	

	Lopez: You’ve hit on a key piece of Mickey’s DNA as a cop. What makes her different from so many other cops on television is the level of compassion and empathy that she has. We’ve seen it time and again, especially when it comes to mothers. While I think attempted murder is a bridge too far with Crystal, it’s not a stretch of my imagination to think that Mickey, at the very least, would check up on that kid. That’s just very much who she is.



	

					Kevin Alejandro
									Courtesy of Justine Yeung/CBS
	




	
		Station 42 was facing some very serious budget and resource issues before this crossover. Are there going to be repercussions for Manny demanding a fire truck that could have potentially been stolen by three convicts?	

	Guggenheim: This crossover exists almost as its own piece. We are tracking some of the character things through these two episodes, but what’s happening with 42 isn’t really addressed in the crossover. You can kind of just drop in without having too much information.


	
		Sharon (Dianne Farr) does show up in the crossover, but we don’t learn anything more about what she’s done with that giant bag of money. What can you tell us about what’s next for that storyline and how it’s going to play out on “Fire Country”?	

	Guggenheim: Sharon has done a bad thing for good and noble reasons, but it’s going to come back to bite her. That’s something that’s going to play out over the next several episodes, beginning with Episode 6.


	
		For “Sheriff Country,” we’ve been dodging the elephant in the room, which is Mickey’s Season 2 premiere confession that she regrets not giving Boone a chance. Is that going to become relevant in the next few episodes?	

	Lopez: It will 1,000% become relevant. Cassidy [Michele Weaver] witnessed that confession. Boone witnessed it. All of those emotions are churning under the surface through the first chapter of our Season 2 and they are going to bubble up in a big way. They will have to be dealt with in ways that I think will force Mickey and Boone into a new dynamic that’ll change their working relationship and their personal relationship moving forward, maybe forever.


	
		Have you started thinking about the next crossover yet? If ‘90s action movies were the inspiration for this one, what genre of film will you be queueing up for the next one?	

	Guggenheim: I thought it would be really nice to flip the order for the next one and have “Fire Country” come first, and then “Sheriff.” That’s been my only thought so far.

	Lopez: I like that idea as well. We’ve talked a little bit about that. I’ve taken a beat to say, “We work for Jerry Bruckheimer: Let’s do a Bruckheimer movie.” That’s where “Con Air” came from. It doesn’t hurt that we usually get a little more money than we ordinarily would for the crossovers. Our attitude is to go big or go home, but I will say this: the crossover romance you cited, whether it’s Mickey and Manny or Tex and Skye, is a really fun fixture that we’re going to see going forward. Maybe John Hughes movies, with a little bit of the jock going out with the nerdy emo girl.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.



	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: ‘Fire Country’ and ‘Sheriff Country’ Bosses Break Down the Crossover Episode, ‘Con Air’ Influences and the Potential Romance That Wasn’t on the Page

title: Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
description: In the pilot of “Suits,” the briefcase that springs open during a job interview is full of marijuana, and it stays that way in the show’s Korean an
body:
In the pilot of “Suits,” the briefcase that springs open during a job interview is full of marijuana, and it stays that way in the show’s Korean and Mongolian remakes. In Japan, the drugs became money, because drugs can’t be shown on Japanese TV, according to Linfield Ng, VP of format sales and production, Asia at NBCUniversal Formats, which licenses the show.

	Ng gave the example at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei, where he shared a stage with Fukaya Shunsuke, head of new format sales, Europe at TBS Television, for a session on how formats get adapted market by market. Emily Chang, who heads the financial news team at Taiwan’s Videoland and produces “Shark Tank Taiwan,” moderated.
	

	“But the concept is the same. Again, that did not change the DNA of the show,” Ng said.

	The same thinking applied to “SNL Korea,” which dropped the musical segment because Korea already has a glut of music and countdown shows. Producers there also asked to soften or skip the U.S. show’s politically pointed cold open at sensitive moments, replacing it with topical material. “We just make slight changes to adapt to the local sensitivity and the local landscape,” Ng said. On “Suits,” every legal case is localized while the core story of the man with no law degree stays intact.

	NBCUniversal has made more than 25 versions of “Top Chef,” and runs a “Top Chef” summit that brings producers from different countries together to trade notes on challenges, shooting styles and what works where. Ng, who joined the company in 2011 after senior stints at BBC Worldwide, Endemol Asia and Warner Bros. Pictures, said his Singapore-based team holds pre-production calls with local partners weeks or months ahead, goes on set with a producer during the shoot and reviews early episodes before they air. Asian versions often add celebrity panels and more behind-the-scenes drama, which he said is agreed well in advance. “So there will never be any surprises where it comes to us, it goes on air, and go like, ‘What is that?’” Ng said.
	

	Fukaya, who joined TBS in 2009 and spent 12 years in production before moving into format sales, pointed to “Sasuke,” known internationally as “Ninja Warrior,” TBS’s biggest format hit with local versions in 25 countries.

	“‘Ninja Warrior’ has a truly universal theme – a human versus giant obstacles – that you can express in one line, and anyone can understand it regardless of country or culture,” Fukaya said.

	TBS keeps a brand guide for the show, separate from the production bible, that defines it as an Olympics for unknown athletes built on serious sportsmanship. Local changes are measured against that concept. When the U.S. and the U.K. wanted a head-to-head version, TBS built a derivative race format, and Fukaya said every new variation gives the company more ways to sell the brand. Host-driven talk shows, by contrast, rarely work as formats, since what TBS licenses is the framework, rules and game, and the banter between particular hosts can’t be reproduced abroad.

	Co-development has been a growing part of TBS’s push since the broadcaster declared two years ago that it was starting its first global year. Fukaya made two such shows with U.K. distributor All3Media International, “Lovers or Liars?” in 2024 and “Tono” a year later, serving as business and creative producer on both. In “Lovers or Liars?” four couples take the stage, only one of them genuine, and a panel tries to spot the real pair from clues such as watching them sing or dance together.

	When the U.K. side proposed ballroom dancing, Fukaya found himself stuck between the two teams, since couples dancing that way isn’t part of Japanese culture. He asked the British creators why they wanted it. The answer was body contact, which helps reveal which couple is real, so the team settled on choreography with plenty of touching.

	“When cultures clash, I think it’s best for the person standing in the middle to confirm what the creative intent is, and find the point of contact there,” Fukaya said. Asked by Chang whether he ballroom dances himself, he laughed and said he couldn’t.

	TBS typically airs its co-developed pilots in late-night slots, and Fukaya said ratings in that window matter less than the fact that a show has been produced and broadcast on a terrestrial network rather than pitched on paper. Some of those late-night pilots are now starting to sell well overseas. “I can’t share the details yet, but I think there will be news soon,” he said.
	

	Ng said Japan always tests its pilots at midnight. “So how much of a rating you can get at midnight timeslot is actually very challenging,” he said.

	On the buying side, Ng’s third-party pickups include Korea’s “Hidden Singer” and “Drive Thru-Oke” and Spain’s “Crush.” In 2026 alone, NBCUniversal Formats added three Asian formats: Korea’s “Unboxing the Flavours,” a cooking show that started life on YouTube; TBS’s “Action Arena,” which Ng likened to a studio-based arcade game; and Chukyo TV’s “Save Money” from Japan. He looks for a clear structure, scalability across budgets, a distinct selling point, and formats that are budget- and sponsor-friendly. “Because in the U.S., many a times, it is all funded by the networks, but in Asia, it’s always sponsors first,” Ng said.

	NBCUniversal Formats has sold more than 40 format brands across Asia, and in 2025 alone had 39 seasons across 17 territories. Ng said rights deals are often split by region: the company may take Asian rights while an owner such as TBS keeps Europe.

	Some formats don’t cross over at all. NBCUniversal acquired MBC’s “Dad! Where Are We Going?” and loved it, Ng said, but found it couldn’t work in Europe, where celebrities won’t put their children on TV for privacy and security reasons. Entertainment and game shows account for about 59% of the formats that sell well globally, according to a 2026 K7 report Ng cited, compared with about 40% in Asia. But game shows don’t work in Korea, so his team never pitches them there. Mongolia, meanwhile, buys only what suits its market rather than the biggest U.S. or Asian hits.

	Ng’s advice to Asian creators was to do their research first and know what sets their show apart. “You’ve got to grab them within the first one to two minutes,” he said. Asked by Chang which elevator offers a one-minute pitch with him, Ng said, “You just got to find the right elevator.”

	Chang put two Taiwanese shows to him. Of Videoland’s night-market competition format, Ng said he enjoyed it but questioned how many countries have a street-food culture big enough to support a local version. He pointed instead to TVBS’s beauty show “Nu Ren Wo Zui Da,” which has been adapted. “Which woman around the whole world doesn’t want to look better?” Ng said.
	

	Chang also traced the origins of her own show: “Shark Tank,” licensed by Videoland from Sony Pictures Television, began as Nippon TV’s “Money Tigers” in 2001 before becoming “Dragons’ Den” in the U.K. and “Shark Tank” in the U.S., and has since landed in more than 50 countries. The Taiwan version had to persuade its U.S. and U.K. partners, with polling and market data, that local viewers needed on-screen captions the original’s clean look doesn’t use.

	Fukaya, who joined the advisory board of the Format Recognition and Protection Association (FRAPA) in 2026, said the group sets criteria for where a format’s protected idea begins and ends, since proving copying in legal terms is difficult. Building an exact replica of “Ninja Warrior’s” Warped Wall would be a clear violation, he said.

	Ng said buying an IP means learning from the owner’s mistakes, and that NBCUniversal would never again partner with a company that copies. “No one wants to buy a copy version,” he said.

	TBS’s “Action! No Reaction” is now under option in over 10 territories across Europe, and Fukaya said buyers are asking TBS above all for comedy game shows, driven by the success of “Documental,” “LOL,” “Freeze” and TBS’s own “Takeshi’s Castle.”

	“You just have to know your market, and you just have to basically think globally and act locally,” Ng said.

schema.headline: Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest

title: ‘Silenced Nights’ and ‘You Are the Film’ to Bookend Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival
description: The 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) will open with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and close with Ueda Makoto’s Ja
body:
The 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) will open with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and close with Ueda Makoto’s Japanese comedy-drama “You Are the Film.” 

	The festival will screen 254 films from 34 countries across its competitive and non-competitive sections.

	The festival runs Nov. 28–Dec. 5 in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, under the theme “Influx.” “Silenced Nights,” which bowed at Toronto, will receive its Indonesian premiere on opening night. “You Are the Film” picked up the White Raven Award at this year’s Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival.
	

	“In line with the theme ‘Influx,’ this year JAFF wants to look at how currents of change affect our lives and the way we understand one another. Amid a social climate full of uncertainty and instability, cinema gives us the chance to listen to different experiences and see issues from other perspectives,” said Budi Irawanto, festival president of JAFF.

	Ten features will vie for the Golden and Silver Hanoman Awards in the main competition, with Dita Gambiro, Riar Rizaldi and Shan Zuolong on the jury. Two of the contenders are first features from women filmmakers. China’s “A Girl Unknown,” directed by Zou Jing, won the Fipresci Prize in Cannes’ Critics’ Week this year. Singapore’s “Ah Girl,” from Priscilla Ang Geck Geck, took the Youth Jury Award at Rotterdam, and its lead actress won the Firebird Award for best actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival.

	Also in the main competition are Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s “9 Temples to Heaven,” Jeremias Nyangoen’s “Black Coffee,” Kawajiri Masanao’s “Cherry and Virgin,” Aung Phyoe’s “Fruit Gathering,” Lê Bảo’s “Hearing,” Arvin Belarmino’s “Ria” and Mejbaur Rahman Sumon’s “Roid.”
	

	On the local front, 10 Indonesian films will compete in the Indonesian Screen Awards across 10 categories, from best film and director through to original music and poster design. The field includes Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” which claimed the Busan Award Special Jury Prize at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, and Ravi Bharwani’s “Secrets,” which will world premiere in Yogyakarta. Ferdinand Almi’s “Shattered Vows,” Ariani Darmawan’s “Jani Be Good” and Andrew Kose’s “Mate’s Rate” are also in the running. Sharifah Amani, Tanigaki Kenji and Yoon Ga-eun make up the jury.

	Shorts are the focus of Light of Asia, where 21 titles compete for the Blencong Awards, while the Netpac Awards consider only debut and sophomore features. Viewers will get a vote of their own through the new Amar Bank Audience Choice Award, which picks a favorite from the Light of Asia selection.

	Also new this year are the JAFF Awards, which will recognize individuals, communities and institutions that sustain Asian cinema through work ranging from production and financing to archiving, exhibition and knowledge-sharing.

	“JAFF was born from a community spirit, and over two decades we have seen how a single encounter can open the way for a film’s or a filmmaker’s journey. The JAFF Awards come from the same belief: that Asian cinema grows through the work of many connected people,” said festival director Ifa Isfansyah.

	Gelanggang Inovasi dan Kreativitas (GIK) UGM serves as venue partner for the awards.

	Outside competition, the Panorama section gathers 12 features and five shorts from leading Asian directors. They include Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s “All of a Sudden,” Lav Diaz’s “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” Hur Jin-ho’s “The Assassin(s),” Yoon Dan-bi’s “The World Before,” Edmund Yeo’s “The Age of Goodbyes” and John Torres’ “The Remotes.” Asian Perspectives offers 26 features and 28 shorts, and the Indonesian Film Showcase has five local features.

	The 15-title Rewind strand revisits three Studio Ghibli classics from Miyazaki Hayao: “Spirited Away,” “My Neighbor Totoro” and “Howl’s Moving Castle.” Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s “Cure,” Yeon Sang-ho’s “Train to Busan” and Yasmin Ahmad’s “Mukhsin” are also on the slate, as are a pair of 2000s Indonesian teen romances, Nasri Cheppy’s “Eiffel…I’m in Love” (2003) and Hanny R. Saputra’s “Heart” (2006).
	

	“Asian cinema keeps moving forward through new voices, a willingness to experiment with form, and stories that stay close to people’s lives. We put together this year’s program to bring that diversity to audiences, including opening new conversations through films we already know,” said program director Alexander Matius.

	The Cinematic Concert, back after four previous editions, will see Grrrl Gang perform live against scenes from five shorts screening at the festival.

	Sponsor partnerships shape several strands. Amar Bank presents Undercurrent, a special screening program of Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana” and Kimura Taichi’s “Fujiko,” the latter a winner of Udine’s Golden Mulberry Award and the New York Asian Film Festival’s Uncaged Award for best feature. Cinema XXI returns as main venue partner at Empire XXI Yogyakarta and is backing JAFF Kids and the festival’s Inclusive Screening strand.

	TikTok Film Circle will pair TikTok creators chosen from Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam with professional film critics in a film analysis workshop. The Asian Film Awards Academy, meanwhile, is co-presenting five Hong Kong titles in the Hong Kong Film Gala Presentation.

	On the industry side, JAFF Market runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center, with six programs: JAFF Future Project, JAFF IP Connection, Talent Day, the Film & Market Conference, Market Screening and Film Lab.

	JAFF21 is backed by Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture through its Dana Indonesia Raya program. Tickets go on sale via TipTip from Nov. 21.

title: Swiss Labor Exploitation Drama ‘Enjoy Your Stay’ Lands in Indonesia, Directors Hope It Speaks for Migrant Workers
description: “Enjoy Your Stay,” the Berlin Film Festival drama from “Goliath” director Dominik Locher and Filipino filmmaker Honeylyn Joy Alipio, has been acqui
body:
“Enjoy Your Stay,” the Berlin Film Festival drama from “Goliath” director Dominik Locher and Filipino filmmaker Honeylyn Joy Alipio, has been acquired by Indonesian distributor Falcon and has its Indonesian premiere at Jakarta World Cinema.

	The film follows Luz, an undocumented Filipina cleaner at a Swiss luxury ski resort.

	“We heard about [stories of] Indonesian people working in nail salons in Swiss cities during our research. That’s even the worst situation in some cases, and we were really hoping that this movie could also speak for Indonesian people,” Locher says.
	

	Luz, played by Mercedes Cabral, may lose custody of her children to her husband back home. To prevent that, she works extra hard and, lured by the legal document and higher pay promised by a Swiss gangmaster, becomes a labor trafficker herself. The reality turns out to be a pipe dream. Locher calls the world it exposes “the dirty side of the Swiss postcard.”

	Alexis Manenti also stars. Close Up Films produced the film, with JBA Production co-producing and Be For Films handling sales.

	Locher and Alipio, who co-wrote and co-directed the film, first met at the Busan International Film Festival. When Locher later set out to tell a story about “people who live in the shadow of Switzerland,” he reached out to Alipio, who agreed to collaborate.

	Alipio trained under Filipino artist Armando “Bing” Lao and works with his “found story” approach, in which filmmakers merge real-life cases into fiction. The pair researched on site at Swiss luxury resorts, talking to undocumented workers from countries including Serbia, Sri Lanka and the Philippines.
	

	Alipio has run into the assumption herself: one of Locher’s neighbors once asked if she was his cleaner. Locher corrected the neighbor – she was his colleague.

	“As a Filipina, I cannot help but feel sadness and shame. I do not want the Filipinas to be portrayed as cleaners, but that is our reality. It was a hard pill to swallow,” Alipio tells Variety.

	She still finds the partnership beautiful, because she and Locher represent the two countries in the story and, together, amplify the voices within it.

	It was Alipio, Locher says, who insisted from the start that Luz not be reduced to a victim because she’s undocumented, “because she must be a very ambitious woman. Otherwise she would never be in Switzerland.”

	That ambition tests her loyalty to her Filipino colleagues, who support each other like sisters.

	After its Berlin world premiere in February, “Enjoy Your Stay” had its Asian premiere at the Cinemalaya Philippine Independent Film Festival, where the filmmakers held a panel with an organization that supports undocumented workers. In Switzerland, where the film will screen publicly on Nov. 22, Locher and Alipio organized a special screening exclusively for undocumented workers. Screenings were fully booked and drew rave reviews from Filipino viewers, many of whom said the film captured their reality.

	“We hoped that [it] would be a movie [people] enjoy watching, but also a movie that stirs up discussions on how to treat one another,” Locher says. Alipio, he adds, once said she hopes that in 50 years, the story the film tells will no longer happen in real life.

	The pair’s next project, “Partner Zone,” which Variety first reported in February, follows a Swiss ESG (environmental, social and governance) auditor to the Philippines to examine a gold mine. Switzerland refines 50%-70% of the world’s annual gold supply.

	“Dom and I have already established a working dynamic. We have an ambition to create more films dedicated to the world’s marginalized people,” Alipio says.

	The duo are still at the research stage and plan to start scripting in 2027, with 90% of the shoot set for the Philippines and the rest in Geneva.

title: CJ Group’s Miky Lee Hailed as ‘Godmother of K-Culture’ as She Receives Asian Hall of Fame Lifetime Achievement Medal
description: Miky Lee, vice chair of Korea’s CJ Group, was handed the Asian Hall of Fame’s Centennial Medal of Lifetime Achievement in Los Angeles. K-pop pionee
body:
Miky Lee, vice chair of Korea’s CJ Group, was handed the Asian Hall of Fame’s Centennial Medal of Lifetime Achievement in Los Angeles. K-pop pioneer Lee Soo-man did the honors.

	Lee Soo-man, the SM Entertainment founder who is now key producer at A2O Entertainment, reminded the audience that Miky Lee had introduced him at the same event a year earlier and called him the godfather of K-pop. “Well, tonight, I’d like to return the favor,” he said. “If I am the godfather of K-pop, then Miky Lee is the godmother of K-culture.”
	

	The Asian Hall of Fame gives the medal to inductees it sees as people of strong character who have raised the bar in their industries, made a cultural mark and worked across racial lines. Miky Lee was recognized for more than 30 years of connecting Korea with audiences abroad through film, music and television.

	The two have been friends for more than 50 years. Lee Soo-man said he first met her when he was a college student who was already a well-known singer and radio and TV host, and she was still a middle schooler. “But even then, she was already the boss,” he said.

	He also told the audience about a phone call he got from her a few years ago while he was in Dubai. She told him to wait for her, then flew in from the U.S. and arrived the next day. He didn’t say what the visit was about. “I’ve learned over the years that it’s very difficult to say no to Miky Lee,” he said.

	Looking back to 1995, when CJ was still known as a food company, Lee Soo-man said: “Korea was hardly a major player in the global entertainment industry. But Miky saw something others didn’t.” He said she helped steer CJ’s DreamWorks investment that year, helped transform Korea’s film industry through CGV, and played a part in turning the MAMA Awards and KCON into worldwide platforms.
	

	“Culture is like oxygen. We may take it for granted, but we cannot live without it,” Miky Lee said in her acceptance speech.

	She was born in Knoxville, Tenn., and raised in Seoul, and she said that belief came from her grandfather, who founded both CJ and Samsung and liked to say, “No culture, no country!” She and her brother Jay took those words to heart at what was then a food business. “We’ve been entertaining people’s mouths. Why not their eyes and ears, too?” she recalled them saying.

	She said the DreamWorks deal was a chance to learn from the best, not a grab at Hollywood glamour. After it came CGV in 1998, Korea’s first multiplex, then a move into cable TV and the launch of production house Studio Dragon.

	She said Mnet was created to give a new generation somewhere to discover homegrown music. Nearly 85% of the songs aired on Korean television were once American pop, she said, but by the 2000s the balance had reversed. The MAMA Awards and KCON later carried that community to cities including Bangkok, Hong Kong, Los Angeles and Tokyo. “‘Music Makes One.’ That was the dream. And the fans brought it to life,” she said.

	Among the Korean filmmakers she has worked with, she named Park Chan-wook, Bong Joon Ho, Lee Chang-dong and “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk. She also pointed to Lee Isaac Chung, “KPop Demon Hunters” director Maggie Kang and Celine Song as filmmakers whose work proves that stories drawn from Asian cultures can travel far beyond them.

	“Our greatest legacy is not simply what we have accomplished, but the opportunities we create for those who come after us,” she said.

	Miky Lee was an executive producer on Bong’s “Parasite,” which in 2020 became the first film not in English to take the best picture Oscar, winning four Academy Awards in total. KCON launched in the U.S. in 2012 and has grown from a K-pop festival into a convention that also covers Korean food, beauty and lifestyle. The MAMA Awards started in 1999 as the Mnet Video Music Awards. More recently, CJ ENM launched the First Light StoryHouse label to back projects from Asian creators, with direct investment and co-production starting from early development.

	The Asian Hall of Fame is an educational and research institution that recognizes Asian and Indigenous legacy. Its 22nd induction ceremony also honored Blackpink’s Rosé and Japanese baseball great Nomo Hideo. Guests included Korean hip-hop artists Tiger JK and Yoon Mi-rae, X Japan leader Yoshiki, Kang, Academy Museum of Motion Pictures director and president Amy Homma, writer-director-producer Lisa Joy, Locarno Film Festival president and Luma Foundation founder Maja Hoffmann, and early Google board member and investor Ram Shriram.

body:
2 Skydivers Dead
                          Collided Mid-Air During Jump

                              November 6, 2026
                            5:40 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Two skydivers in California died Friday after they reportedly collided mid-air during a jump.
      
    
            According to the Riverside County Fire Department, firefighters arrived on the scene of "traumatic injuries involving two skydivers."
      
    
            Officials say the collision happened on Cereal Street near Corydon Road. It appears the skydivers collided midair about 50 feet above the ground.
      

            RCFD wrote on X ... "Both patients suffered major injuries and were transported by ground ambulance for further care."
      
    
            The skydivers were taken to Inland Valley Medical Center in Wildomar, but died at the hospital.
      
    
            The skydivers' identities have not been released.
